title: The Drug Control Program's Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112 on interchanging an authorized generic
rule_summary: Department of Public Health Drug Control Program Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, Dispensing Authorized Generics, dated January 14, 2022 and addressed to Massachusetts pharmacies and pharmacists, states that the term 'authorized generic' is defined in 21 CFR 314.3 and is most commonly used to describe an approved brand name drug that is marketed without the brand name on its label; that other than the fact that it does not have the brand name on its label, it is the exact same drug product as the branded product; and that an authorized generic drug is marketed under the brand name drug company, or another company with the brand name company's permission. It states that because the authorized generic is identical to the brand name drug, it is not specifically listed in the Orange Book, but it is considered to be therapeutically equivalent to its brand name drug, and that therefore a pharmacist may interchange a prescription written for a brand name drug with its authorized generic version provided that the prescriber did not indicate 'no substitution' on the prescription. It states that if a pharmacist is not able to determine if drug products are interchangeable using the FDA listing of authorized generics, the pharmacist should contact the manufacturers, distributors, or re-packagers.
exam_relevance: Tests that an authorized generic, although not specifically listed in the Orange Book, may be interchanged for a prescription written for its brand name drug unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution', and that the statement is Drug Control Program guidance rather than regulation.

authority.name: Department of Public Health, Drug Control Program: Circular Letter DCP 22-01-112, Dispensing Authorized Generics (January 14, 2022)

exceptions: The circular's statement that a pharmacist may interchange an authorized generic applies provided that the prescriber did not indicate 'no substitution' on the prescription.
common_confusions: Ruling out an authorized generic because it is not specifically listed in the Orange Book. The circular states that it is considered therapeutically equivalent to its brand name drug and may be interchanged.
Interchanging an authorized generic on a prescription on which the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'. The circular's statement is conditioned on no such indication.
Treating the circular as a regulation. It is Drug Control Program guidance addressed to Massachusetts pharmacies and pharmacists.
